'''Bérengère Dubrulle''' (born 1965) is a French astrophysicist whose research involves the study of [[turbulence]] and [[Vortex|vortices]] in [[fluid dynamics]] and [[magnetohydrodynamics]], and their application in modeling [[planet formation]] and [[climate change]].{{r|world}} She is a director of research for the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]], and the director of the [[École de physique des Houches]].{{r|ijc}}

==Education and career==
Dubrulle was born in 1965 in [[Dieppe]], on the north coast of France. She was a student at the [[École normale supérieure de jeunes filles]] from 1985 to 1989, earning a master's degree in [[quantum mechanics]] in 1987 through [[Pierre and Marie Curie University]] and defending a Ph.D. in astrophysics in 1990 through [[Toulouse III - Paul Sabatier University]] under the direction of {{ill|Jean-Paul Zahn|fr}}. She completed a [[habilitation]] in physics in 1996, through [[Paris Diderot University]].{{r|cv}}

Meanwhile, she became a scientist (''chargée de recherche'') in the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]] (CNRS) in 1991, was promoted to director of research in 2000, and was named as director of research, exceptional class, in 2021.{{r|cv}} She is affiliated with the Sphynx laboratory (''Systèmes Physiques Hors-équilibres hYdrodynamiques éNergie et compleXité'', out-of-equilibrium Systems and Physics - HYdrodynamics - eNergy and compleXity) at [[CEA Paris-Saclay]].{{r|sphynx}} Since 2020, she has also been director of the [[École de physique des Houches]].{{r|ijc|houches}}

==Recognition==
Dubrulle was the 2008 recipient of the {{ill|Madame Victor Noury Prize|fr|Prix Madame-Victor-Noury}} of the [[French Academy of Sciences]],{{r|ijc}} and was named female scientist of the year as a recipient of the 2022 [[Irène Joliot-Curie Prize]].{{r|world|ijc}} She received the [[CNRS Bronze Medal]] in 1993, and the [[CNRS Silver Medal]] in 2017.{{r|ijc}}

The [[European Geosciences Union]] gave Dubrulle the 2021 Lewis Fry Richardson Medal "for outstanding contributions to the field of geophysical and astrophysical turbulence, and for a unique approach to the study of experimental turbulent flows using statistical mechanics".{{r|lfr}} She was named a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] (APS) in 2023, after a nomination from the APS Division of Fluid Dynamics, "for seminal contributions to the theory of fully developed turbulence and astro- and geophysical fluid dynamics in general, and in particular, for illuminating intermittency and the role of multiple states in turbulent flows".{{r|faps}}
